passages.ENG-P0187: The Mahabodhi Temple stands as one of the most revered and historically layered monuments in the Buddhist world, embodying both spiritual awakening and architectural endurance. Located in Bodh Gaya, the site marks the exact spot where Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment nearly 2,500 years ago. According to tradition, the young seeker meditated under a peepal tree for three days, culminating in a moment of profound realization that transformed him into the Buddha, or the "Enlightened One." Recognizing the sanctity of this event, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka commissioned the first shrine at this location in the 3rd century BCE, making it one of the earliest formal Buddhist monuments. Over time, however, the structure underwent several transformations. The present temple, with its soaring pyramidal tower rising approximately 55 metres, largely dates to the Gupta period (5th-6th century CE), a time often associated with artistic and architectural refinement in the Indian subcontinent. Beyond its historical origins, the temple complex is rich in symbolic elements. Adjacent to the shrine stands a descendant of the original Bodhi Tree, under which the Buddha meditated. At its base lies the Vajrasana, or "Diamond Throne," believed to mark the precise spot of enlightenment. The temple itself is enclosed by intricately carved stone railings, some dating back to the 2nd century BCE, depicting motifs from Buddhist lore and everyday life. Yet, the journey of the Mahabodhi Temple has not been uninterrupted. With the decline of Buddhism in India after the 8th century, the site gradually fell into neglect and even changed custodial hands. By the late 19th century, it required significant restoration, which was undertaken with the involvement of both Burmese patrons and British officials. A prolonged legal and religious struggle eventually restored its status as a Buddhist shrine, though its management continues to reflect a shared religious legacy. Today, the Mahabodhi Temple is not merely an architectural relic but a living centre of pilgrimage, drawing devotees from across the globe. Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002, it continues to resonate with spiritual vitality while bearing silent testimony to centuries of devotion, conflict, and renewal. L	To be part of Zimbabwe’s “Born Free” generation was to be handed a promise: that your life
would no longer be shaped by colonial rule. Skin colour would not dictate the right to vote,
learn or work. For Simukai Chigudu, born in 1986, six years after independence, that promise
was stamped on him from the very beginning: “Your name, Simukai, it means to stand up,” his
father, a former liberation fighter, tells him.
Yet, as Chigudu reflects in his compelling memoir, the end of colonial rule does not mean
freedom from historical events and how they reverberate in everyday life. He tells two
interlinked stories: Zimbabwe’s brutal war of independence, and his own search for belonging
in the years that followed. It is a wide-ranging, restless book, passing through Uganda,
Rwanda, Ireland and Mexico City. Yet at its centre are Zimbabwe and Britain, “former colony
and metropole”, and the unfinished business between them.
Chigudu’s parents, who became part of the growing post-independence black middle class,
enrol him in elite private schools. There, he acquires what he calls a “delicate, papery accent”,
plays “white people’s sports” and learns the codes of respectability that promise safety but not
belonging. He comes to appreciate early on that to be black is to be defined by others. Black
Zimbabweans dismiss him as a “salad” for his adopted white habits (such as eating salad).
White Zimbabweans call him a soutpiel, or “salt penis”; for having one foot in Africa, one in
Europe, his genitals “[dangling] in the Mediterranean Sea”. In Britain, a student labels him
“the whitest black man” they know. The burden of his generation’s inheritance is expressed
most powerfully in descriptions of his grandfather’s murder — “they shot him in cold blood and
jettisoned his remains in a shallow pit” — and his father Tafi’s torture under the racist
Rhodesian government. Tafi joined the armed struggle and spent years in exile. “I felt the
weight of history, my life as the gift of his having survived colossal violence,” Chigudu writes.

passages.ENG-P0190: India's mental health crisis is both vast and underappreciated. According to the Global Burden of Disease study, nearly 197 million Indians - roughly one in seven - live with some form of mental disorder. Depression and anxiety alone affect over 90 million people, yet for most, professional support remains out of reach. For decades, stigma was considered the primary barrier. By 2025, however, the conversation had shifted. Stigma, while still present, was no longer the central obstacle. The more urgent questions had become practical ones: how does care actually function once someone seeks help, and what happens when symptoms escalate? The answer, increasingly, lies in integrated, end-to-end models of care. India's mental health systems were historically built around isolated touchpoints - therapy sessions existed separately from psychiatric care, digital tools operated independently of clinical oversight, and hospitalisation sat at the extreme end of the spectrum, disconnected from what came before and after. Individuals and families were expected to navigate these transitions alone, often during periods of acute vulnerability. Effective systems, experts argue, must allow individuals to move fluidly between levels of support - digital guidance, outpatient care, crisis intervention, and structured inpatient settings - without losing continuity of care. Technology has played a critical role in widening access. The government's Tele-MANAS platform, upgraded in 2025 with a multilingual interface in ten regional languages and an AI-powered chatbot named Asmi, has expanded mental health outreach significantly. Private platforms such as Wysa, Amaha, and Lissun are using AI-driven tools to reach underserved populations. However, a key lesson from 2025 is that access alone is insufficient. Digital tools can open doors, but they cannot substitute for trained professionals or structured clinical care. Looking ahead, India's mental healthcare challenge in 2026 is one of consolidation rather than experimentation. Hospitals, outpatient centres, digital platforms, workplaces, and community networks must function as parts of a coherent whole. Equally important is recognising families not merely as informal caregivers but as active stakeholders in recovery. The opportunity is significant - India has the chance to build a mental healthcare system that is preventative, responsive, and continuous, one that meets people where they are. (Source: National Mental Health Survey of India)

II. The space traveller had been floating in the vast emptiness of space for what seemed like an eternity. The
stars that had once seemed so bright and beckoning now appeared distant and unwelcoming. The traveller's
mind began to wander, and he found himself considering the philosophical implications of Warren's thought
experiment.
Warren had proposed that if a space traveller were to be placed in a state of suspended animation for a long
period of time, during which he would be cut off from all contact with the outside world, he would no longer
exist as a person. Instead, he would be replaced by a new entity, one with identical memories and personality
but without any connection to the original person.
The space traveller found himself pondering the implications of this thought experiment as he floated in the
infinite void of space. Was he still the same person he had been when he first embarked on his journey? Had his
consciousness been transformed by the endless expanse of space and time?
As he drifted through the darkness, he began to notice a strange sensation in his body. His limbs felt heavy and
unresponsive, and he realized that he had been in a state of suspended animation for longer than he had
anticipated. The realization filled him with a sense of unease and dread, and he wondered if he had been
transformed into a new entity, one without any connection to his former self.
The traveller's mind began to race as he contemplated the implications of this realization. Was he still the same
person he had been before his journey began, or had he been transformed into something new and unknown?
Was his consciousness still intact, or had it been replaced by something else entirely?
As he grappled with these existential questions, the traveller's body began to fail him. His heart rate slowed, and
his breathing became shallow and laboured. He realized that his journey had come to an end, and that he was
about to be transformed once again, this time into something entirely different.
With a final gasp, the traveller's consciousness slipped away, leaving behind a lifeless husk floating in the
endless void of space. The implications of Warren's thought experiment suddenly became all too real, and the
traveller realized that he had been transformed into something new and unknown, something that transcended
the boundaries of space and time.

III. At some point in life, we all experience the sting of loneliness. During such times, we often feel unsupported and
become despondent, succumbing to worry and anxiety. Life's pendulum swings between moments of joy and times of
sorrow, and in the midst of turmoil, we may find ourselves anxious, fearful, and even angry. Caught in a downward spiral,
it becomes challenging to break free from the web of negativity and pessimism we weave for ourselves.
In these moments of helplessness, we seek an anchor to weather life's storms. Saints and mystics suggest a way out,
advising that when our boat is caught in a storm, we should avoid creating another storm by adding to the turmoil. The
key to navigating through the storm is to remain calm and still, anchoring ourselves in God.
The scriptures of various faiths remind us that the divine is always with us, offering support. However, we often feel
lonely because we are accustomed to living at the level of our physical senses. Our physical eyes and ears are limited to
perceiving only a certain range of matter and frequencies. Despite this, God is always beside us, guiding us through life's


difficulties. To experience God, we must transcend the physical senses, which is where the practice of meditation comes
in. A spiritual Master can teach us to still the mind, transcend physical senses, and focus our attention on the inner
spiritual world, revealing a realm of joy, peace, tranquility, and bliss.
God, being all consciousness and spirit, cannot be experienced through physical senses. To truly experience the divine, we
must follow the path laid out by saints and spiritual Masters. They found God in silence. By withdrawing from the outer
world's chatter, sitting in silence, and stilling the body and mind, we can transcend physical body consciousness and
embark on an inner journey. This journey allows us to commune with God and experience His presence firsthand. The
more we sit in silence and focus within, the closer we get to God, fulfilling life’s purpose of merging our soul back into
the Creator.
As we experience God's presence, we anchor ourselves in the stability of His love. Life's challenges no longer overwhelm
us; instead, we ride the wave, knowing that 'this too shall pass.’ The pangs of loneliness dissipate when we realize that we
are never truly alone. Regular meditation and connection with the inner Light help us recognize His presence in our lives.
God's love, ever-present, carries us through life's ups and downs, providing strength to face any circumstance with hope
and positivity.

IV.	Dowry-related fatalities reliably trigger choreographed cycles of legislative indignation,
prosecutorial posturing, and performative collective mourning — yet the socioeconomic
substructure that inexorably generates such violence emerges from each episode of public outrage
structurally uncontested, institutionally reinforced, and culturally resanctified. This recursive
contradiction constitutes perhaps the most consequential and deliberately unacknowledged market
failure embedded within India's social economy: a polity that statutorily criminalises dowry while
systematically legitimising its operational logic through euphemistic reclassification — financial
extractions repackaged as familial gifting, status capitalisation, or economically rational
compensation accruing to the male-headed provisioning household. Matrimony in India functions
less as a voluntary interpersonal arrangement than as a sophisticated multi-dimensional
institution — concurrently executing caste boundary enforcement, intergenerational capital
transfer, gendered labour allocation, and hierarchical social mobility negotiation. Within this
institutional architecture, transactional expectations are not peripheral aberrations but
structurally determined outputs of the system's own internal logic. Violence, therefore, resists
analytical disaggregation from the institution itself; it represents the most visible downstream
manifestation of legitimised economic asymmetry, operationalised within household units where
women disproportionately absorb unremunerated care labour, sacrifice professional capital, and
bear asymmetric responsibility for relational preservation — a systematically feminised
productivity cost that neither markets price nor policymakers adequately account for. The
institution's more insidious coercive mechanisms operate beneath the threshold of juridical
visibility entirely: the manufactured social panic surrounding unmarried women of advancing age,
the structural delegitimisation of alternative domesticity arrangements, and the categorical
expectation that intimacy, economic security, and social belonging must be accessed exclusively
through sanctioned matrimonial channels. What presents phenomenologically as autonomous
individual choice routinely operates within profoundly constrained decision environments where
viable structural alternatives have been methodically denied institutional recognition, resource
allocation, and cultural legitimacy. Legislative intervention, however procedurally indispensable,
addresses symptomatic manifestations while leaving foundational determinants operationally
undisturbed. Substantive reform demands something considerably more architecturally disruptive
— the deliberate redistribution of care infrastructure, the institutional scaffolding of collective
living arrangements, and the political willingness to systematically decouple human dignity,
belonging, and security from their near-total dependence upon the privatised matrimonial
household as civilisation's singular legitimate organising unit.
passages.ENG-P0194:
I. The Supreme Court judgement on the right to menstrual hygiene as an integral part of the
constitutional right to life and dignity provides a long-desired direction towards destigmatising
an essential bodily function and ensuring basic care. While observing that the lack of basic
facilities and the stigma around menstruation directly affect girls’ health, education and privacy,
the bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and R Mahadevan directed all states and Union territories
to ensure within three months that every school has gender-segregated toilets, and
biodegradable or reusable sanitary pads are provided for free to adolescent girls along with safe
disposal facilities. The court also asked the governments to incorporate gender-responsive
curriculums in schools and train the staff in assisting menstruating pupils.
The apex court’s judgement and directions expose the socio-cultural and religious taboos
perpetuated by patriarchal norms. Period shame is every girl’s burden. The event of puberty, a
milestone in human physiological evolution, is celebrated in many Indian traditions. But period
ostracisation is so deeply prevalent in many sections that the victims of such misinformed
belief and gender aggression are eventually socialised to become its carriers. The troubling
apportioning of ‘shame’ continues through generations. For girls born into economically
weaker families, sanitary pads are a luxury. Government schools, an ideal place to clear the
misconceptions for both girls and boys, ignore this duty. To aggravate the insensitive attitude,
their administrators often force hapless teenage girls to explain clothes stains as period blood,
stripping them of dignity.
By one estimate, around 2.3 crore girls drop out of school annually on account of lack of
adequate toilets and menstrual provisions. The launch of the Union Health Ministry’s
Menstrual Hygiene Scheme in 2011 was a landmark attempt to destigmatise menstruation by
giving girls aged 10 to 19 subsidised pads and menstrual education. But it left out the adolescent
girls who are out of school. The right to education is as fundamental a right as the right to live
with dignity. With the Supreme Court spelling out the nuances of the constitutional right of
young girls in detail, it’s time to fill the gaps. For that, government and private schools have to
act in a timebound manner. And all three tiers of government have to ensure that awareness of
the right as well as the health basics reach all sections of India—in every generation.

institutional-assurance
passages.ENG-P0195: Sami trains in the alley off Al-Wahda Street, in Gaza, lifting chunks of concrete above his head, deadlifting car doors, and doing pull-ups from the frames of bombed-out windows. There is no gym anymore - only the skeletal remains of a neighborhood and a few iron bars salvaged from the wreckage. He keeps a pair of tattered training gloves in his pocket, a gift from his cousin Yusuf, who was killed in an airstrike. The gloves are split at the seams and darkened by sweat. He turns them over sometimes, as if inspecting a wound. Before the war, Sami had a routine. He worked part-time at a hardware shop, portioned his meals with surgical precision - eggs, chicken, rice - and saved for months to buy imported protein powder, clutching each tin like treasure. He trained at a gym near the beach until his shirt clung to him like a second skin. His dream was not fame or escape. It was simple: to grow bigger, to carve himself into something unbreakable. Now the chicken is gone. The eggs are scarce. He eats lentils, bread when there's bread, sardines from dented cans. He once found a row of canned sardines in the charred remains of Abu Khalil's Minimarket, clawing through plaster dust and shattered glass to reach them. That haul lasted him two weeks. He records everything in a notebook tucked into the sole of an old boot - reps, sets, rough calorie guesses - the ink running from sweat, but written nonetheless. On a WhatsApp call, he angled the phone so the narrator could read one entry: "Deadlift: 7 reps, 60 kg (I think - maybe more). Food: 100g lentils." There is a boy named Khaled - barefoot, maybe ten - who watches Sami lift and asks, "Why do you still do it?" Sami grins and says, "Because I can." But after Khaled walks away, something twists in Sami's chest. He wonders if lifting is theft - strength stolen from those who can't. Yet each time the bar digs into his shoulders, the shame burns off. He thinks: maybe what he offers is simply the sight of someone who hasn't quit. Maybe that is enough. The narrator closes with Camus: One must imagine Sisyphus happy. To bulk, to build, to lift - when the world wants you erased - is its own kind of refusal. Sami pushes the rock up the hill. It falls. He grips it again. (Source: Guernica magazine)

I. Having meaningful connections in the workplace is essential for personal and organisational success. Most of
us form these bonds naturally, as we spend a significant amount of our lifetimes at work.

After leaving college, many people in their 20s move to new cities for career opportunities, where they face the
task of creating a brand new social circle from scratch. The workplace becomes an ideal place for people to
connect.

Activities like grabbing drinks after work, playing team sports or just sharing meals serve as opportunities to
form connections with co-workers. These interactions not only help combat feelings of isolation, but also add a
sense of camaraderie and support to the daily work routine.

However, as individuals reach milestones like getting married or starting a family, their priorities in life
naturally shift. The fun after work hangouts and casual meetups start taking a backseat to family commitments
and home responsibilities.
Consequently, you might find that keeping up with work friendships becomes more challenging over time.
Balancing professional growth and one’s personal life often leads to a decrease in the frequency and depth of
these relationships while still preserving any already-established connections. There is a difference between
typical co-worker relationships and true friendships. Generally speaking, people we work with are not
necessarily friends. In our personal lives, it often takes years of building trust to bring someone into our circle
of friends. Yet many of us do develop friendships with colleagues we have worked alongside — often for years.
For instance, I've made friends at work whom I respect and trust immensely — one of my best friends is
someone I met on the job. Our friendship continued to thrive long after I left that workplace. That said, do I
share my deepest, darkest secrets with work friends? Nope. So then, is a work friend worth it? In short, yes —
even relationships with weaker ties can be beneficial. But it depends on the depth and nature of the relationship.

Friendships can result in substantial benefits. When employees are happy, engaged and productive, and the
organisation is meeting their individual needs, they are more likely to meet their full potential. Connection and
community are essential to the workplace. They help us create a sense of belonging, strengthen our
psychological contracts with our employers and help drive us to be motivated and efficient. Strong relationships
can facilitate communication and advice-sharing among co-workers.

However, it's important to note workplace friendships can have a downside. Friendships at work can be
problematic due to rumours of relationships, nepotism and favouritism, to name a few. The concept of “work”
and “play” can often conflict when career goals intersect or worse when there is a conflict. That said, many of
these issues can be mitigated with clear boundaries and communication.

passages.ENG-P0197:
I. Diwali déjà vu is nice. We are looking forward to the lights and festivities. And Diwali
déjà vu is maddening. In NCR and many other of the country’s urban centres, a large
constituency of unwell citizens and those with children and pets who are scared by
firecrackers or find breathing hard in smoke’s wake, are dreading the onset of bad air. The
apex court itself has been deeply engaged in this conversation for a decade, as have several
govt bodies, civic organisations, business lobbies etc. But here we are yet again, relitigating
the same issues all over again, just as we did last year and the year before that.

Doesn’t the NCR ban on firecrackers hurt the spirit of Diwali? Shouldn’t green firecrackers
at least be permitted? But is there any such thing as a firecracker that’s green? Isn’t it a
false impression being created that these are environmentally safe? But where is the data
showing that it’s the firecrackers that cause the bulk of Diwali pollution? Round and round
we go, as if determined to make no progress whatsoever.

If the stop, start, kneejerk measures are helping, we are not doing any proper measuring of
it. When GRAP restrictions delayed the recarpeting of a Delhi runway last year, we didn’t
tally the emissions of the thousands of waiting and hovering aircraft. BJP to AAP, the past
years have seen different political parties pass the buck, without wholehearted focus on
finding a way out. If NCR is set on a green firecrackers path this Diwali, it will be with the
full foreknowledge that all kinds of pollution will fly through this net. Testing infra is
absurdly inadequate to cover all the points of sale.

The consensus that’s been missing so far is not going to drop down from the smog
tomorrow either. Public policy expert Michael Munger underlines how the adoption of the
US constitution itself defied preexisting rules for consensus, and how lucky this was for
America. He sees the role of constitutions as enabling politics, which in turn is a process
of deciding on rules, such that even the losers accept as legitimate. When the tree-lined
Cheonggyecheon was brought back to life in central Seoul, it meant fighting back
disagreements as much as a vast elevated highway. But it’s a vision that’s paid back South
Korea a million-fold. Restoring India’s rivers, forests, air and soil to health will certainly
not be cost-free. But just as certain is that the costs of failing will be nightmarishly higher.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/257425/
passages.ENG-P0198: For more than two decades, India's information technology industry built something genuinely admirable: a world class services engine that became the back office of the global economy. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra collectively generated hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue, employed millions of engineers, and powered an entire ecosystem of technical education across the country. Then came the AI revolution - and the industry was caught almost entirely unprepared. The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was not a sudden shock. It was the visible peak of a transformation building since deep learning went mainstream after 2015. But Indian IT firms, locked into low-risk service contracts and investing less than three per cent of revenues in R&D compared to ten to twenty per cent at global technology companies, had neither the incentive nor the institutional culture to see it coming. By the time the alarm was impossible to ignore, the frontier had already been claimed by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a set of well-funded Chinese laboratories. What followed was a period of genuine reckoning. The traditional pyramid model, in which armies of junior engineers churned out standardised code with revenues scaling directly with headcount, began to crack. AI could now perform many of those base layer tasks: routine code generation, testing, data processing, and documentation. At the same time, the growth of over 2,000 Global Capability Centres meant multinationals that once outsourced wholesale were now building substantial in-house teams in India. The existential question became unavoidable: if Indian IT cannot build the AI, and its traditional clients are increasingly building their own teams, what exactly is the industry's role? Four structural failures explain why Indian IT missed the frontier AI race entirely. The first is the services trap. (Source:The Statesman)

XXVI. People explain their decision to write in remarkably different ways. One claims that writing
offers refuge from an intolerable world; another insists that it is an instrument through which
reality may be mastered. Both explanations appear convincing until we notice that escape and
mastery are by no means unique to literature. Withdrawal may be achieved through solitude,
ritual, intoxication, silence, or even oblivion. Power may be pursued through wealth, political
authority, or physical force. Why, then, should one seek either liberation or dominion through
language? Beneath these diverse motives lies a more fundamental commitment—a decision
that precedes every poem, novel, essay, or philosophical treatise. To understand literature,
therefore, we must ask not merely why people write, but what kind of relationship with the
world writing presupposes.
Human consciousness occupies a peculiar position within existence. The world does not cease
to exist when no one looks at it, yet neither does it become a meaningful world until someone
encounters it. Mountains, rivers, abandoned cities, and forgotten stars possess neither
significance nor arrangement simply by existing. Their unity is not an intrinsic feature
waiting to be discovered like an object beneath a cloth. Rather, unity emerges through
consciousness itself. A ruined cathedral becomes an emblem of history only because someone
perceives continuity between broken stone, passing centuries, and present reflection. A
coastline becomes a landscape because countless isolated sensations are gathered into a single
intelligible experience. In this sense, consciousness does not manufacture reality, but neither
does it merely receive it. It organizes, discloses, and relates what would otherwise remain an
immeasurable abundance of disconnected presence.www.lptedtech.com
Yet this role immediately reveals its own limitation. However indispensable consciousness
may be in revealing the world, it never possesses the authority to bring that world into
existence. One may close one's eyes before the sea, but the tide does not suspend itself in
obedience. One may forget an ancient forest, but memory neither nourishes nor destroys its
trees. Consciousness therefore occupies an uncomfortable position. It experiences itself as
necessary for meaning while simultaneously recognizing itself as unnecessary for existence.
The world exceeds every act through which it is interpreted. Whatever significance we bestow

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
upon things remains inseparable from our presence, whereas the things themselves persist
with complete indifference toward the one who interprets them.
Much of artistic creation originates precisely within this tension. The artist seeks not merely
to observe reality but to overcome the unsettling awareness of being simultaneously
indispensable and dispensable. By composing a symphony, painting a portrait, or writing a
novel, the creator appears to impose coherence upon fragments that otherwise remain
dispersed. Relationships are selected, emphasized, omitted, and arranged until necessity
seems to emerge where contingency once prevailed. At first glance, this appears to satisfy the
desire for essentiality. Yet the satisfaction proves remarkably unstable. The completed work
immediately acquires a peculiar independence from the activity that produced it. The painter
continues to discover alterations that might still be made; the composer imagines different
orchestrations; the novelist mentally rewrites sentences already printed. Creation never
appears entirely complete to its creator because the creator remains imprisoned within the
very process through which the work came into being.
This paradox becomes clearer if we distinguish making from encountering. When we
encounter an object not of our own making, it confronts us with an existence that resists our
intentions. Its independence grants it objectivity. But the creator rarely experiences such
resistance toward the work just produced. Every brushstroke recalls the hesitation preceding
it; every paragraph evokes discarded alternatives; every decision remains transparent because
it originated within the creator's own deliberation. The finished work therefore never achieves
the opacity characteristic of objects encountered rather than produced. It continues to appear
less as an independent thing than as the visible residue of countless subjective decisions. To
perceive it is simultaneously to remember producing it.
No art exposes this condition more dramatically than literature. A sculpture occupies space
regardless of whether anyone contemplates it. A melody may linger unheard, awaiting
performance. A written work, however, exists in a strangely suspended condition. Ink resting
upon paper constitutes only the material possibility of literature, not literature itself. The
literary work emerges only when language becomes an active event within another
consciousness. Reading is therefore not passive reception but continuous reconstruction. Each
sentence generates expectations concerning those that follow; each paragraph revises or
frustrates anticipations established by the previous one. Meaning unfolds not as a fixed object
waiting intact inside the text but as an achievement produced through the reader's movement
across it.
For this reason the writer confronts a limitation unknown to many other makers. A
cabinetmaker may immediately use the table just completed. An architect may inhabit the
house whose construction has ended. The writer, however, cannot become the first genuine
reader of the work just written. Familiarity with every intention, revision, hesitation, and
discarded possibility prevents the necessary distance through which the text might acquire

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
genuine objectivity. What the reader encounters is discovery; what the writer encounters is
recollection. The writer inevitably arrives too early, carrying memories that obstruct surprise.
The literary work therefore belongs neither entirely to its author nor entirely to its reader.
Left unread, it remains an unrealized possibility. Read without the author's labour, it would
never have existed at all. Its existence is completed only through an encounter in which one
consciousness offers possibilities that another consciousness freely realizes. Writing is thus
neither an escape from the world nor an attempt to dominate it. It is an invitation extended
toward another freedom, an appeal for a collaboration in which meaning becomes possible only
because neither participant can produce it alone.

I	The cosmos is an edgy place. We are on the far edge of a rapidly expanding Universe, hurtling
into nothing. Earth is now further away than it was when you began to read this sentence,
from the place where, at the time of the Big Bang, everything started. We have to put it that
way, but it is wrong. For at the moment of the Big Bang, neither space nor time existed. They
were forged in the explosion. Everything that has happened in space and time happened on
the far fringes. The process of creation and innovation is delegated to the margins. This
sounds poetical. It is. But it is not just poetry. It’s a statement of the way things are and the
way things happen in all domains, from evolutionary biology to religion. They understood this
well in the Middle Ages. The abode of the stars — the stellatum — marked the edge of the
visible cosmos. Beyond this was the rotating Primum Mobile — the prime mover, whose motion
powered everything else. The ultimate edge was the engine driving all Earthly action.
Evolutionary innovation happens at the edge of genetic orthodoxy, at the edge of an
established population, and typically at the edge of a landmass: hence the exuberant biological
creativity seen on islands, where new challenges are faced and old inhibitions relaxed. Take
the St Kilda archipelago, for instance, in the heaving green sea off the outer isles of Scotland.
It once housed a community of embattled farmers and seabird hunters. They were all
evacuated in 1930, leaving behind two species of mice, both unique to the islands. The St Kilda
house mouse, whose life depended on its coalition with the humans, went extinct within a few
years. But the St Kilda field mouse, uninhibited by house mice, cats and humans, blossomed
and changed. It doubled in size and became an enthusiastic flesh-eater, prowling the beaches
and headlands for dead birds. Edges were fecund on St Kilda — at least for field mice. They
always are. Indeed, nothing else is. Sexual reproduction itself is another good example of the
creativity of edginess. It involves organisms and their gametes crossing the boundaries of the
organism, meeting in the no-man’s land of a fallopian tube, or water, or air, and producing
there something different from either of the parents. Sex is a machine for generating novelty.
The newly gestated organism bursts across the edge of its mother, becoming fully itself. [Word
Count: 407]

SECTION I
I.	In recent years, the global conversation around productivity has undergone a marked
transformation. Once equated with relentless output and longer working hours, productivity is
now increasingly understood through the lens of sustainability, mental health, and long-term
efficiency. This shift has been accelerated by the pandemic, which blurred the boundaries between
professional and personal life, compelling organisations to reassess their expectations from
employees.
Remote work, initially perceived as a temporary compromise, has revealed both its promise and
pitfalls. While it offers flexibility and autonomy, it has also fostered burnout by dissolving
temporal limits on labour. Employees report working longer hours, not because they are compelled
to, but because the absence of physical separation makes disengagement psychologically difficult.
Consequently, productivity measured merely by hours logged has become an unreliable indicator
of actual value created.
Moreover, cognitive science has begun to challenge the myth of sustained concentration. Research
suggests that human attention functions in cycles, not as an uninterrupted stream. Attempts to
enforce constant focus often result in diminishing returns, undermining creativity and problem-
solving. Progressive organisations, recognising this, are experimenting with shorter workweeks,
asynchronous communication, and output-oriented assessments.
However, sceptics argue that such reforms risk normalising inefficiency and eroding
accountability. They contend that flexibility, if unregulated, may privilege certain employees while
disadvantaging others whose roles demand synchronous collaboration. The challenge, therefore,
lies not in abandoning productivity metrics but in refining them to reflect meaningful contribution
rather than performative busyness.
Ultimately, redefining productivity requires a cultural recalibration—one that values depth over
immediacy and outcomes over optics. Whether institutions can achieve this balance remains
uncertain, but the conversation itself signals a departure from industrial-age assumptions about
labour.
passages.ENG-P0202: The U.S. has allowed its waiver of sanctions on Iran's Chabahar port to lapse, indicating that India is now at a crossroads on how to proceed with the port as a key connectivity initiative. Barring a belated waiver renewal, New Delhi must choose between accepting sanctions and abandoning its $620 million investment, or proceeding with the project and risk strict U.S. sanctions. India's "start-stop" engagement with Iran on developing a facility at the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar goes back decades, and Prime Minister A.B. Vajpayee signed an MoU for the project in 2003. However, U.S. pressure on India to postpone plans aimed at stopping Iran's nuclear programme led to construction delays. The Manmohan Singh government was unable to make much progress either, but continued work on the Zaranj-Delaram highway to connect the Iran-Afghanistan border crossing to Kabul. After the 2015 JCPOA, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government signed a trilateral agreement with Iran and Afghanistan to advance trade and aid via Chabahar port and a highway into Afghanistan. Chabahar's importance grew as ties with Pakistan deteriorated and it restricted India's transit access to Afghanistan. However, fate intervened again as U.S. President Donald Trump walked out of the JCPOA, and began a "maximum pressure" campaign against Iran by re-implementing all sanctions. While India was forced by the U.S. to give up Iranian oil imports and plans for the rail line, the U.S. built a "carve-out" for Chabahar, allowing India to send wheat and medical supplies to Afghanistan. That carve-out is now at an end, with the Trump administration giving Delhi until this month to "wind-down" its operations. Since November 2025, India has withdrawn personnel from Chabahar, prepaid its $120 million investment commitment, and is considering transferring its stake in the Shahid Beheshti Terminal to an Iranian company. The West Asia war has complicated the situation, and it is unclear when India will be able to re-engage with Iran or rebuild Chabahar. Temporarily dropping the project may seem pragmatic. However, Chabahar is just one of several India's independent decisions that the U.S. has thwarted, including demands to stop buying oil from Iran, Venezuela, and Russia. Giving in on Chabahar will not just end India's connectivity plans with Iran, Central Asia and Afghanistan, but also damage its claims of sovereign autonomy and its ability to pursue an independent foreign policy. I.	War is as old as humanity. Long before it became a matter of law or strategy, it was written into
our myths and instincts: the urge to dominate, the struggle for survival, the fall from paradise into
conflict. As the author Robert Ardrey once observed, we are not only animals; we are armed ones.
In modern times, the reality of war has become impossible to ignore. The photographs of
Hiroshima’s ruins, the televised images from the Vietnam War, the viral pictures from the Bucha
massacre in Ukraine and the latest livestreamed bombardments of Gaza all make clear what
earlier generations could more easily conceal or forget. War is not only the threat of violence. It is
the collapse of moral and political order: a moment when the rules of coexistence fall apart, laws
twist into something else, and human life loses its value, or takes on a new one. Yet even in such
devastation, responsibility does not disappear. To inherit war is to inherit the responsibility to
restrain it. In democracies, that burden is said to be shared — rooted in consent, exercised through
representation. And still, while war may be as old as humanity, democracy is not, and that
difference reshapes the questions citizens must ask.
What happens when the gravest of political acts — the decision to kill — is taken without the
citizens’ assent? That is the paradox of what I call the silent mandate: leaders treat the people’s
silence, which is structurally imposed, as if it were consent, turning absence into acquiescence. It
is the point where democracy keeps its name but loses its meaning. If conflict is the most serious
act a political community can undertake, shouldn’t it face a higher bar than ordinary political
decisions in a democratic state? And even if a conflict seems to meet the conditions of a ‘just war’ —
if such a thing exists — it may still be illegitimate if those in whose name it is fought were never
asked.
In democracies, wars are rarely directly fought by civil society itself, but they are financed by it,
and money carries its own moral weight. The decision is made not on the battlefield but within
institutions that claim to speak for the people while avoiding their voice. Some doctrines allow for
war in so-called ‘supreme emergencies’. But can such reasoning ever suffice in a democracy, where
legitimacy should flow from the will of the people? Such silence is dangerous. It binds us, citizens,
to the consequences of war while denying us any role in deciding whether it should be waged.
[Sociology; Word Count: 426]

SECTION I
I.	The theory of natural selection, as articulated by Charles Darwin and independently
formulated by Alfred Russel Wallace, is often celebrated not merely for its originality but for
its decisive explanatory economy. What distinguishes it from earlier speculative accounts of
life is its capacity to resolve, with remarkable conceptual restraint, the long-standing puzzle of
purposiveness in nature. Where earlier frameworks were compelled to invoke design or pre-
established harmony to account for the precise adaptation of organisms to their environments,
the principle of selection renders such assumptions not only unnecessary but intellectually
excessive.
Darwin’s insight did not emerge fully formed but was preceded by a careful engagement with
the problem of variability. Observing how human breeders selectively amplified desirable
traits, he recognised that transformation within species required no mysterious force, only the
consistent retention of certain variations over others. Yet the critical difficulty lay in
extending this logic to nature itself, where no conscious selector appeared to operate. It is here
that Darwin’s engagement with Malthus becomes pivotal: the realisation that organisms
reproduce in excess of what their environments can sustain introduces an unavoidable
condition of competition.
This condition, which Darwin termed the “struggle for existence,” is frequently misunderstood
when reduced to crude images of predation. Its true significance lies in the far subtler and
more pervasive competition among individuals of the same species, where even marginal
advantages determine survival. The evaluative force of Darwin’s argument rests precisely on
this point: what survives is not the strongest in any absolute sense, but the most suitably
constituted relative to specific conditions. In this sense, selection is less an event than a
continuous filtration.
Such a view compels a reconsideration of adaptation itself. Rather than being evidence of prior
intention, adaptation emerges as the cumulative outcome of innumerable eliminations, where
non-advantageous variations are quietly discarded. The elegance of this explanation lies in its
refusal to posit any guiding intelligence; instead, it locates order in repetition. Over successive
generations, this repeated selection produces structures that appear purposive, though they
are nothing more than the residue of what has endured.
It is this relentless emphasis on repetition—on the continual preservation of the relatively
better suited—that constitutes the true strength of the theory. By grounding complexity in a
simple, recurring process, Darwin not only displaces earlier metaphysical explanations but
also establishes a framework within which both diversity and precision can be understood
without recourse to external design. The enduring power of natural selection lies, therefore,
not in any single insight, but in the consistency with which it explains the emergence of form
through the repeated survival of the suitable.
Source: On Darwin’s Theory of Natural Selection — explanatory scientific text

I.	The human mind is a restless blend of past memories, future anxieties, and current desires. It
is often likened to a “monkey” jumping from thought to thought. Natural human qualities such
as desire, fear, attachment, and comparison drive this constant inner race. When desires go
unmet, or we face the loss of what we are attached to, the mind suffers.
Sri Thannerpalli Krishnan Swamy explained the spiritual concept of “Jalasandhi” — the
confluence of two rivers, or a river meeting the ocean — and compared it to a profound
metaphor for the human condition. Water never stays still and always finds a way around
obstacles. In the same way, the mind remains in a state of flux. At a confluence, separate
streams merge into one current. Ideally, our diverse experiences and emotions should become
a source of calm. Yet, humans are often distracted by bodily desires and lose sight of the
higher purpose of birth.
Continuing this exploration of the mind’s nature, controlling it is difficult due to the three
gunas (qualities) inherent in the body: Sattva (honesty and peace), Rajas (passion and anger),
and Tamas (impatience and ignorance). According to the laws of Karma, humans often
struggle with lower levels of Sattva and higher levels of Rajas and Tamas. This imbalance
leads to ahankara (false ego), where the spirit soul becomes bewildered and mistakenly
identifies itself with the perishable body.
Given these challenges, to overcome these spiritual hurdles and focus on the atma (soul), the
scriptures suggest three primary paths. First, one must cultivate Sattva guna. Second, one
should practise moderation in worldly affairs, maintaining just enough attachment to fulfil
duties while focusing on spiritual growth. Finally, one should seek “Acharya Parampara” —
the company and blessings of the great teachers. By serving those who have attained wisdom
through discipline and penance, one can alleviate one’s own obstacles and sins, leading to a
clearer, more peaceful life. [Psychology; Word Count: 315]

V. Were it not for the tragic circumstances of his death, Y Puran Kumar would have been
seen as an example of social mobility and of the upholding of the Indian Constitution’s
promise of equality. He was a Scheduled Caste (SC) Indian Police Service officer of the
Haryana cadre; his wife, Amneet P Kumar, is an SC IAS officer, and his brother-in-law is an
MLA in Punjab. On the face of it, Kumar and his family had reached the upper echelons of
government and politics. His suicide and the eight-page note he leaves behind, which alleges
systemic discrimination, including by senior IPS officers, however, casts a shadow on that
image. It also raises disturbing questions about entrenched biases that cramp and distort
institutional spaces. These questions must be addressed, not evaded.

The allegations of “mental and administrative torture” and “caste-based discrimination,
public humiliation, targeted mental harassment and atrocities” by senior officers in Haryana
in Kumar’s dying declaration must be probed. The National Commission for Scheduled
Castes (NCSC) has directed the Chief Secretary and Director General of Police, Chandigarh,
to submit an action taken report in seven days. The state government and police must
investigate Kumar’s suicide urgently, in a transparent manner. The temptation to close ranks
in the face of public and judicial scrutiny must be avoided. Issues of embedded prejudice and
discrimination and their effect on the mental health of those at the receiving end are too
important to be brushed under the carpet. This must be a moment for the police to reflect and
introspect.

Caste is a proven fact in crime and punishment in India. The Status of Policing in India
Report (2025) by Common Cause and Lokniti found that victims of torture are “most often
from marginalised communities” and that police personnel across states see certain SC and
ST communities as “criminal”. The survey also found that “one in every four Scheduled
Caste (SC) police personnel think that Dalits do not get justice”. The caste-based, and even
casteist, nature of policing in India is an unfortunate remnant of a colonial structure that
urgently needs to be consigned to the past. Doing so, however, is easier said than done, and
requires police forces — particularly at the leadership level — to be open and sensitive as
they turn the searchlight inwards. Kumar’s death and his allegations must not be swept under
the institutional carpet. The Haryana police cannot allow discrimination to go unchecked and


unpunished within.

not easy to find in ordinary light.” When his daughter Clara’s beloved black cat Bambino
disappeared while she was convalescing in a sanatorium, Mark Twain put out the ad in the
New York American and spent days receiving strangers with abandoned black cats in the hope
of finding Bambino among them. The cat returned on his own, but it was no secret in New York
that the American writer loved his daughter, and Bambino, with equal fervour.

That they occupy a special place in the lives of their humans is no secret. But separated by
centuries and continents, the spurt in litigation and mediations in India’s capital over pets and
strays only goes to show that the law is just beginning to catch up with what the heart has
always known: That animals matter — not as assets, but as companions. And, in some
circumstances, they are the bone of contention or caught between adversaries. Take, for
instance, a civil suit filed in 2023 by an advocate against his neighbours in south Delhi. The
reason: Their pet had chased him, leading him to fall and fracture his wrists. When TMC MP
Mahua Moitra broke up with lawyer Jai Anant Dehadrai, the bitterness spilled over into a
custody tussle over their beloved Rottweiler, Henry.

It may seem trivial to some, absurd even, but these disputes, at their core, are declarations of
how much trust is conveyed through a wag of a tail or the flick of a feline ear. In lonely, crowded
urban metropolises, pets provide the kind of unstinting comfort that few can. Neighbours fight,
lovers part, but what lingers is the bond with the creature left in between. Reforms to Australian
law last month recognised this: For the first time, in cases of separation, Australian courts will
factor in emotional attachment when determining pet ownership. As Delhi courts navigate this
tricky terrain, it is a reminder that love, no matter how small or furry, always leaves a trail.

II. Land use patterns and roads in the central Indian landscape were disrupting genetic connectivity of two large
herbivores Gaur and Sambar, according to a first-of-its-kind study of large herbivores at a landscape scale in
India. The findings of the study done by the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS) indicated high
genetic differentiation, suggesting that the animals were present in small populations with little to no gene flow.

Central India, like other areas of conservation concern, faced threats from growing linear infrastructure such as
highways, railway lines and changes in land use patterns, expanding road network, mining activities and other
development projects. Such infrastructure hinder animal movement, creating fragmented populations confined
within small habitat patches disconnected from each other.

To investigate genetic connectivity, a team of researchers from NCBS collected 1,144 gaur and 756 sambar
faecal samples from tiger reserves and wildlife sanctuaries in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Following a
genetic species identity, 921 samples were identified as gaur, while 504 samples were determined to be of
sambar. The team investigated whether the species comprised a single contiguous population across the
landscape or were fragmented into distinct groups, using next-generation sequencing (NGS) and combination of
population and landscape genetic tools. The study was the first to examine the genetic connectivity of large
herbivores at a landscape scale in India. It analysed the genetic diversity of gaur and sambar, which was crucial
for any species to adapt to sudden environmental changes, diseases, climate shifts and other stressors. The
findings revealed that gaur was most impacted by land-use and land-cover changes, roads with high traffic and
dense linear infrastructure intrusion. These fragmented gaur populations also showed low levels of genetic
diversity.
Sambar, besides land use-land cover and high-traffic roads, was also impacted by human presence. Though
sambar populations did not show much differentiation, low levels of genetic diversity were concerning.
Researchers speculated that this could be attributed to the large population size of sambar. However, with more
data, genetic differentiation may become evident. Gaur and sambar rank among the top prey species for large
carnivores like tigers. Gaur is the largest wild cattle species and one of the few mega-herbivore species that
inhabit the Indian subcontinent. Although the species was once found throughout the forested areas of India, its
current distribution is restricted to fragmented habitat pockets, primarily in the Western Ghats, the central Indian
highlands and northeast India.

XXVII. The modern painter enjoys a degree of artistic freedom that earlier civilizations could scarcely
have imagined. Subjects once ranked according to social prestige or religious importance have
gradually lost their privileged status. A bowl of fruit, an abandoned factory, a child's toy, or
the collapse of an empire may now claim equal artistic legitimacy. This liberation from
prescribed themes is often celebrated as one of modern art's defining achievements. Yet it has
also produced an unexpected paradox. As painters became increasingly free to depict virtually
anything, many gradually abandoned representation itself. Rather than expanding the
catalogue of subjects indefinitely, they began to question whether painting required a
recognizable subject at all. The historical coincidence is unlikely to be accidental. As artists
acquired unprecedented freedom to represent almost anything, the burden shifted from
obeying convention to determining what deserved representation in the first place.
Abstraction, for many painters, became not merely a rejection of subject matter but an
attempt to escape the exhausting responsibility of choosing among infinitely legitimate
possibilities.
Whether this explanation entirely accounts for the emergence of abstract art remains open to
debate. Many artistic, technological, and philosophical developments undoubtedly contributed
to its rise. Nevertheless, the connection deserves serious attention because it reveals a deeper
problem that extends beyond abstraction itself. Unlimited freedom does not eliminate artistic
judgment; rather, it intensifies it. When nothing is forbidden, nothing is automatically
significant. The painter's problem therefore changes from asking 'May I paint this?' to asking
'Why should this, rather than everything else, be painted?' Freedom, paradoxically, transforms
artistic selection from a technical decision into a philosophical one.
This shift exposes a widespread misunderstanding concerning subject matter. Many suppose
that a subject begins with whatever happens to stand before the easel or with an especially
vivid personal memory. Neither explanation reaches the heart of the matter. A subject begins
when the painter decides that one fragment of experience deserves to be distinguished from
every competing possibility. Such a decision is necessarily an act of valuation. Whether
attracted by colour, rhythm, texture, form, or emotional resonance, the artist has already
judged one object to possess greater significance than countless others equally available for
representation. The completed painting must therefore persuade its viewers that this act of
selection was justified rather than arbitrary—not through external explanation but by

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
enabling them to perceive why this particular subject deserved attention while innumerable
alternatives did not.
The distinction is crucial because artistic success depends upon more than technical execution.
A painting succeeds not simply by depicting an object convincingly but by transforming private
significance into communicable significance. The artist's personal conviction may initiate the
creative process, yet it cannot complete it. If the finished work cannot lead others to recognize
why the selected subject merited sustained attention, the painting remains little more than a
private preference disguised as public expression. Historical traditions may assist this
transformation by supplying widely recognized symbols and meanings, but they neither
guarantee artistic success nor constitute its indispensable foundation.
Communication, however, never occurs in isolation from culture. Every civilization
establishes—often without conscious reflection—a hierarchy of what deserves notice. Artists
inherit these assumptions long before they challenge them. A sacred mountain, an agricultural
landscape, or the unclothed human body may possess profound symbolic force within one
society while appearing visually unremarkable within another. Their significance lies neither
exclusively in the objects themselves nor entirely in the painter's imagination but in a network
of shared cultural associations. Such traditions facilitate artistic communication because they
provide painter and audience with a common language of significance. Yet they remain only
one possible source of shared understanding rather than the only one.
When a culture enjoys confidence in its values, the artist rarely experiences anxiety over
subject matter. Society itself performs much of the work of selection by identifying stories,
rituals, landscapes, and symbols that already possess accepted importance. Under such
conditions, originality lies chiefly in interpretation rather than discovery. The artist exercises
comparatively little freedom, yet seldom confronts uncertainty regarding what deserves
representation because inherited traditions have already answered that question.
Periods of cultural transition create precisely the opposite situation. Shared values weaken,
inherited symbols lose unquestioned authority, and artists acquire unprecedented freedom.
Yet this liberation imposes a corresponding responsibility. Every decision concerning subject
matter becomes an implicit judgment about what society itself ought to regard as meaningful.
The painter no longer merely reflects a cultural consensus but actively constructs one. The
contrast is fundamental: earlier artists inherited significance, whereas modern artists
increasingly establish it through deliberate acts of selection. For this reason, many of the
fiercest controversies surrounding modern painting originated not in questions of technique
but in disagreements over what deserved public attention.
Modern painters have generally responded to this responsibility in one of two ways. Some
have sought guidance beyond themselves by allowing the ordinary experiences of everyday
life—the worker, the marketplace, the anonymous street—to determine what merits artistic
attention. Others have turned inward, treating the language of painting itself—colour,

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
rhythm, texture, and form—as the only reliable source of necessity. Although these
approaches appear fundamentally opposed, both attempt to answer the same philosophical
question: when tradition no longer determines significance, upon what grounds can artistic
selection legitimately claim public importance?
No single answer can finally resolve that question. Different artists, working under different
historical conditions, have answered it differently, and each solution illuminates only one
possibility among many. The purpose of this discussion is therefore not to celebrate
abstraction, condemn tradition, or prescribe a single artistic doctrine. It is instead to
understand why expanding artistic freedom inevitably transforms the nature of artistic
responsibility. The history of modern painting is, above all, the history of artists attempting to
justify—not merely their methods—but their reasons for choosing one fragment of reality over
every other possibility.

V. Supreme Court’s lament about the government not willing to modernise the delivery of the death
sentence – it was hearing a petition to replace death by hanging with lethal injection – needs some
parsing, and continuous discussions beyond cases in court. The death penalty has three debates that run
concurrently. First, whether capital punishment should be abolished. Second, a restrained and diligent
application of the penalty. SC and CJIs have time and again appealed to HCs to be ultra-careful when


sentencing convicts to death. The sentencing itself is harrowing for most convicts, however hardened
the criminal. On death row, it is long years of appeals till death is delivered or the sentence commuted.
The third debate is on the ‘best’ – or ‘humane’ – way to service the sentence.
Neither the debates nor the arguments are new. A British govt commission report in the 1950s exploring
modes of execution said of its goal: any method untried that would inflict death as painless and certain
as hanging but with “greater decency” and without the “degrading and barbarous association with which
hanging is tainted”. The argument against this debate is that there’s no ‘humane’ way; the very decision
is troubling. That discussing ‘best methods’ is in fact, an attempt to protect shared values – the natural
right to life and ‘dignity of death’. The reality, though, is that so long as the death penalty is on the
statute, it must be asked: is hanging the most certain, quickest, and least painful method with minimum
bruising? Should there be options? If so, what?
No method is ‘best’. The world recoiled when Alabama last year used nitrogen gas asphyxia in a global
first as a new mode, claiming death would be instant. Instead, the convict struggled for life for several
minutes – nitrogen was on for 15 minutes. US prisons are exploring new ways because drugs for lethal
injections (sodium thiopental) are difficult to source – countries are ceasing manufacture and banning
export of drugs for capital punishment. US states have re-introduced electrocution and the gas chamber
(hydrogen cyanide). Finding trained personnel is a challenge. Non-medical people carrying out a
medical mode of execution have also seen botched executions. India on its part has a shortage of
hangmen although executions are rare – there can be no worse torture than a botched hanging. To that
end, SC’s point on GOI’s lack of response is on point. It is not alone about policy. It’s a complicated
medico-legal issue. However squeamish it makes one, the question of option is not to be sidestepped.

Night after night I had passed the house (it was vacation time) and studied the lighted square of window: and night after night I had found it lighted in the same way, faintly and evenly. If he was dead, I thought, I would see the reflection of candles on the darkened blind for I knew that two candles must be set at the head of a corpse. He had often said to me: "I am not long for this world," and I had thought his words idle. Now I knew they were true. Every night as I gazed up at the window I said softly to myself the word paralysis. It had always sounded strangely in my ears, like the word gnomon in the Euclid and the word simony in the Catechism. But now it sounded to me like the name of some maleficent and sinful being. It filled me with fear, and yet I longed to be nearer to it and to look upon its deadly work. Old Cotter was sitting at the fire, smoking, when I came downstairs to supper. While my aunt was ladling out my stirabout he said, as if returning to some former remark of his: "No, I wouldn't say he was exactly ... but there was something queer ... there was something uncanny about him. I'll tell you my opinion...." He began to puff at his pipe, no doubt arranging his opinion in his mind. Tiresome old fool! When we knew him first he used to be rather interesting, talking of faints and worms; but I soon grew tired of him and his endless stories about the distillery. "I have my own theory about it," he said. "I think it was one of those ... peculiar cases.... But it's hard to say...." He began to puff again at his pipe without giving us his theory. My uncle saw me staring and said to me: "Well, so your old friend is gone, you'll be sorry to hear." "Who?" said I. "Father Flynn." "Is he dead?" "Mr Cotter here has just told us. He was passing by the house." I knew that I was under observation so I continued eating as if the news had not interested me. My uncle explained to old Cotter. "The youngster and he were great friends. The old chap taught him a great deal, mind you; and they say he had a great wish for him." "God have mercy on his soul," said my aunt piously. Old Cotter looked at me for a while. I felt that his little beady black eyes were examining me but I would not satisfy him by looking up from my plate. He returned to his pipe and finally spat rudely into the grate. (450 words, The Dubliners by James Joyce)

III. Compassion is a central virtue in Buddhism, and it is often seen as a panacea for all problems. The Buddha
himself was known for his boundless compassion, and he frequently taught his followers to cultivate this quality
as a means of overcoming suffering and achieving enlightenment. However, as with any virtue, compassion can
be taken too far, leading to harmful consequences for both the practitioner and those around them. One of the
dangers of excessive compassion is burnout, which can occur when caregivers or other helpers become
emotionally exhausted from constantly putting the needs of others before their own. This is particularly
common among those who work with people who are suffering, such as healthcare professionals, social
workers, and aid workers. In these contexts, the pressure to be compassionate and empathetic can be
overwhelming, leading to emotional exhaustion, depression, and other negative outcomes.
Another danger of excessive compassion is the belief that it gives one a moral authority to intervene in the lives
of others, even when their assistance is not wanted or needed. This can lead to a form of self-righteousness in
which the practitioner believes that they know what is best for others and has a duty to help them, whether they
want it or not. This can be particularly problematic when it comes to issues of cultural sensitivity and respect for
autonomy, as the practitioner may unintentionally impose their own values and beliefs on others. One example
of this is the case of a Buddhist monk in Thailand who became known for his extreme acts of compassion. He

would rescue animals from slaughterhouses and care for them in his temple, often at the expense of his own
health and well-being. While his actions were motivated by compassion, they were ultimately harmful both to
himself and to the animals he was trying to save, as he was not able to provide them with the proper care and
attention they needed. In this case, the monk's compassion led him to act in ways that were not sustainable or
effective, ultimately causing more harm than good.
To avoid these pitfalls, it is important to cultivate a more balanced approach to compassion, one that recognizes
its importance while also acknowledging its potential pitfalls. This might involve setting boundaries around the
amount of time and energy one devotes to caring for others, as well as seeking guidance from experienced
teachers and mentors who can provide guidance on how to practice compassion in a healthy and sustainable
way. Additionally, it is important to recognize that compassion is not a panacea for all problems and that there
are times when other virtues, such as patience, equanimity, or wisdom, may be more appropriate. Ultimately, the
goal should be to cultivate a compassionate heart that is grounded in wisdom, equanimity, and a deep
understanding of the complexities of human suffering. In this way, Buddhists can use compassion as a powerful
tool for alleviating suffering and promoting well-being, without falling into the trap of excessive or misguided
compassion that can do more harm than good.
Source: Winfield, Pamela D. "Medicine or Poison: When Buddhist Compassion Goes Too Far." Aeon
https://aeon.co/essays/medicine-or-poison-when-buddhist-compassion-goes-too-far.

SECTION I
IL	Supposing that nothing else is "given" as real but our world of desires and passions, that we
cannot sink or rise to any other "reality" but just that of our impulses—for thinking is only a
relation of these impulses to one another:—are we not permitted to make the attempt and to
ask the question whether this which is "given" does not suffice, by means of our counterparts,
for the understanding even of the so-called mechanical (or "material") world? I do not mean as
an illusion, a "semblance," a "representation" (in the Berkeleyan and Schopenhauerian sense),
but as possessing the same degree of reality as our emotions themselves—as a more primitive
form of the world of emotions, in which everything still lies locked in a mighty unity, which
afterwards branches off and develops itself in organic processes (naturally also, refines and
debilitates)—as a kind of instinctive life in which all organic functions, including self-
regulation, assimilation, nutrition, secretion, and change of matter, are still synthetically
united with one another—as a primary form of life?—In the end, it is not only permitted to
make this attempt, it is commanded by the conscience of logical method. Not to assume several
kinds of causality, so long as the attempt to get along with a single one has not been pushed to
its furthest extent (to absurdity, if I may be allowed to say so): that is a morality of method
which one may not repudiate nowadays—it follows "from its definition," as mathematicians
say. The question is ultimately whether we really recognize the will as operating, whether we
believe in the causality of the will; if we do so—and fundamentally our belief in this is just our
belief in causality itself—we must make the attempt to posit hypothetically the causality of the
will as the only causality. "Will" can naturally only operate on "will"—and not on "matter" (not
on "nerves," for instance): in short, the hypothesis must be hazarded, whether will does not
operate on will wherever "effects" are recognized—and whether all mechanical action,
inasmuch as a power operates therein, is not just the power of will, the effect of will. Granted,
finally, that we succeeded in explaining our entire instinctive life as the development and
ramification of one fundamental form of will—namely, the Will to Power, as my thesis puts it;
granted that all organic functions could be traced back to this Will to Power, and that the
solution of the problem of generation and nutrition—it is one problem—could also be found
therein: one would thus have acquired the right to define all active force unequivocally as will
to power. The world seen from within, the world defined and designated according to its
"intelligible character"—it would simply be "Will to Power," and nothing else.
Source: Beyond Good and Evil by Friedrich Nietzsche

L	My observations of No. 427, Park Lane did little to resolve the problem that occupied my mind.
The house, separated from the street by a low wall and railing, was easily accessible from the
garden, yet the window itself remained beyond reach. There was no pipe, no ledge—nothing to
assist even the most agile intruder. Still perplexed, I returned to my study in Kensington, my
thoughts unsettled by the contradiction.
Thad scarcely settled in when the maid entered.
“A person desires to see you, sir,” she said.
“Who is it?” I asked.
Before she could respond, the visitor appeared. To my astonishment, it was the same elderly
book collector I had encountered earlier—his sharp, wizened face framed in white hair, his
arms burdened with volumes.
“You're surprised to see me, sir,” he said in a strange, croaking voice.
“T confess that I am,” I replied.
“Well, I’ve a conscience, sir,” he continued. “When I saw you enter this house, I thought I
would step in and assure you that if I seemed gruff earlier, no offense was intended. I am much
obliged to you for picking up my books.”
“You make too much of a trifle,” I said. “But tell me—how did you know who I was?”
“Tf it isn’t too great a liberty,” he answered, “I am your neighbour. My bookshop stands at the
corner of Church Street. You may visit any time. Perhaps you are a collector yourself? I have
British Birds, Catullus, and The Holy War—each a bargain. Five volumes would neatly fill
that gap on your second shelf. It looks rather untidy, does it not, sir?”
His remark was so precise that I instinctively turned to glance at the cabinet behind me.
That single movement altered everything.
When I looked back, the old man had vanished.
In his place stood Sherlock Holmes—smiling calmly across my study table.
For several seconds, I could neither speak nor move. Then the room seemed to darken; a grey
mist swirled before my eyes, and I lost all sense of awareness.
When I recovered, I found myself seated, my collar loosened, the sharp taste of brandy
lingering. Holmes stood over me, a flask in his hand.
“My dear Watson,” he said in that familiar voice, “I owe you a thousand apologies. I had not
anticipated that my reappearance would affect you so strongly.”
I seized him by the arms.
“Holmes!” I cried. “Is it truly you? Can you indeed be alive? Did you escape that dreadful
abyss?”
“Pray, compose yourself,” he replied. “Are you certain you are fit to discuss such matters? I fear
my return has been unnecessarily dramatic.”

“I am quite well,” I said, though my voice trembled. “But I can scarcely trust my senses. To
think that you—of all men—should stand here before me...”
Holmes regarded me steadily, a faint smile still upon his lips.
“Appearances,” he said quietly, “are often deceptive, my dear Watson.”
He paused.
“And what you have seen today—”
He did not finish.

Doyle.

I	In a stretch of desert north of Cairo, a small fragment of jawbone is forcing a rethink of where
the story of modern apes, including humans, may have begun. The fossil belongs to a newly
identified species, Masripithecus moghraensis, which lived about 17 to 18 million years ago
during the Early Miocene. Described in Science, the fossil was found at Wadi Moghra and is
the first definitive ape from North Africa from this time period — pointing to Egypt, and
possibly the wider North Africa—Middle East region, as a key region in the origin of living
apes, helping fill a gap in the early history of crown Hominoidea, the group that includes all
living apes and their last common ancestor. We spent five years searching for this kind of
fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that
something is missing — and North Africa holds that missing piece.
Until now, Early Miocene sites in North Africa had turned up monkeys, but not apes. That gap
helped shape the view that early apes and their close relatives were restricted to more
southern parts of Africa during this period. Younger ape fossils have been found across Africa,
Asia, and Europe, but their relationships and the group's first emergence remain debated.
Masripithecus shows that apes lived in North Africa during the Early Miocene and that the
species was distinct from similarly aged East African apes, suggesting the fossil record has
been missing part of the record of where the earliest branches of the ape family diversified.
Masripithecus combines Masr, the Arabic word for Egypt, with the Greek word for ape. The
species name, moghraensis, refers to Wadi Moghra, where the remains were recovered in 2023
and 2024.
The fossil consists of a lower jaw, but it preserves a combination of features not seen in any
other known ape from this time. The jaw is robust, with large canine and premolar teeth and
rounded, textured molars. This suggests Masripithecus had a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet,
with the ability to process tougher foods, such as nuts and seeds, when needed. That flexibility
would have been useful in a region becoming more seasonal, where climatic shifts in northern
Africa and Arabia made food supplies less predictable. [Word Count: 377]
